analysis.one_liner: Limits lawsuits over false Year 2000 computer-readiness statements to encourage companies to disclose Y2K problems.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on it — it sat in the Judiciary Committee until Congress ended in January 1999 — but a companion Senate bill with the same liability protections became law in October 1998.
analysis.plain_summary: With the Year 2000 bug threatening computers that stored dates as two digits, Congress worried that companies would stay silent about their systems' readiness rather than risk being sued over what they said. This bill made it much harder to win a lawsuit over a false or misleading Y2K statement: a victim would have to prove the company knew the statement was false, meant to deceive, or was grossly negligent. It also presumed that posting a notice on a company's own website counted as adequate warning, raised the bar for defamation claims about Y2K statements, and shielded information companies gave the government about Y2K from public records requests. It carved out statements made directly to consumers at the point of sale and left government regulators free to enforce the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and software makers disclosing Y2K readiness information gain a shield against most lawsuits over statements that turn out to be wrong, so long as they did not knowingly lie. The public also stands to gain if the promised effect holds: freer disclosure of Y2K problems gives everyone more warning about products and services that may fail.

how_it_helps.text: A company or person cannot be held liable for a false or misleading Y2K statement unless the victim proves the statement was material and was made knowingly, with intent to deceive, or with grossly negligent failure to verify it — a much higher bar than ordinary negligence.
Posting a Y2K notice on the company's own website is presumed to be an adequate way of providing notice, when no clearly more effective method is practicable.
Defamation and trade-disparagement claims based on Y2K statements require the victim to prove actual knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard by clear and convincing evidence.

Information companies volunteer to federal agencies in response to 'Special Year 2000 Data Gathering Requests' is protected from Freedom of Information Act disclosure and cannot be used against them in civil actions.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone harmed by relying on a false or misleading Y2K statement — a business or person who bought or planned around a product that was declared 'ready' — bears the cost: they must prove knowing deception or gross negligence rather than simple carelessness. Claimants in defamation suits face an even higher 'clear and convincing' bar, and website posting is presumed sufficient notice even though many people in 1998 had no internet access.
analysis.who_pays_short: Victims of false Y2K readiness claims

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the burden of proof for victims of false Y2K statements from ordinary negligence to knowledge, intent, or gross negligence, making careless false 'we're ready' claims largely lawsuit-proof unless they were egregious.
It presumes that a notice posted on a company's website adequately warned the public, which in 1998 disadvantaged people without internet access.
It shields information voluntarily given to federal agencies from Freedom of Information Act disclosure, reducing public visibility into which systems were reported as non-compliant.

The strongest defense of these trade-offs is that the bill explicitly excludes statements made directly to consumers at the point of sale, leaves contract and warranty rights intact, and does not bind government regulators or enforcement actions — so the most direct consumer harm remains fully actionable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine trade-off rather than a giveaway. Its liability limits are real and would have let some careless Y2K claims escape liability, and the website-notice presumption and FOIA shield favor companies. But the drafters narrowed the shield carefully: consumer sales pitches, written contracts and warranties, and all government enforcement are carved out. Given the national stakes of the Y2K bug, the disclosure-encouraging rationale was credible, and a companion version with the same core protections passed the Senate and was signed into law with bipartisan support.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never came out, dying when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 — though the House action record pointed to a Senate companion, which passed and was signed into law that October.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Burton introduced the bill on July 30, 1998, with 27 cosponsors — 21 Democrats and 6 Republicans — and the text records that all of them joined 'by request,' the method used when a bill is introduced at the administration's request.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on July 30, 1998, and no further committee or floor action ever appears in the record.
The action history notes 'For Further Action See S.2392,' the Senate companion; that bill, the Year 2000 Information and Readiness Disclosure Act, became law in October 1998.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies wanting protection from Y2K lawsuits ended up with it anyway, since the Senate companion became law in October 1998. Consumers were not left worse off by this bill's failure: the companion law carried the same carve-outs for consumer sales statements and government enforcement.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies, via the Senate companion that became law

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all joining by request.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 30, 1998 and never reported it out or scheduled any action before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican, but 21 of the 27 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill was introduced by request — suggesting administration backing — so the bill's support crossed party lines heavily.

industries.note: The bill shields companies from most lawsuits over false or misleading Y2K readiness statements, while the stated purpose is that this shield would free them to disclose problems the public needs to know about. Consumer sales statements are excluded from the shield, keeping point-of-sale claims fully actionable.
Raising the fault standard and easing notice requirements reduces the pool of Y2K-related claims insurers would have to pay, at the cost of victims' ability to recover for careless false statements.
